# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 40 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic Equivalence)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** P.Mich. 130, Shepherd of Hermas 40 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_040_page_001.jpg

---

## Mandate 6, Part 2 — One Chance for Repentance

**40:1** "Lord," I said, "there is one more thing I need to ask you." "Go ahead," he said. "I've heard some teachers say," I told him, "that there's no repentance apart from the one we received when we went into the water at baptism and had our previous sins forgiven."

**40:2** "What you heard is correct," he replied. "That is how it stands. Anyone who has had their sins forgiven should never sin again — they should live in purity from that point on. But since you want to understand everything precisely, let me explain this too, so that no one has any excuse — whether they are believing now or will believe in the future. Those who have already believed, or who will believe later, have no second repentance of sins available to them. What they do have is forgiveness for sins committed before they believed."

**40:3** "For those who were called in earlier times, the Lord did provide for repentance. Because the Lord knows every heart and foresees everything, he understood human weakness and the devil's many tricks for harming and corrupting God's servants. Out of compassion, the Lord took pity on his creation and put this repentance in place — and authority over that repentance was given to me."

**40:4** "But I am telling you," he said, "if after receiving that great and holy calling someone is tempted by the devil and falls into sin, they have one opportunity for repentance. But if they keep sinning and repenting over and over again — that does them no good. A person like that will barely survive."

**40:5** "I feel as if I've come back to life hearing you explain this so clearly," I told him. "Because I know that if I stop adding to my sins, I will be saved." "Yes, you will be saved," he said — "you and everyone else who lives this way."

---

*PNEUMA renders for contemporary clarity and accessibility, capturing the urgency of Hermas's once-for-all repentance doctrine.*
